concept.name: Array Manipulation Techniques

relationships.description: Connects Array Manipulation Techniques to core algorithm patterns in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Core array manipulation techniques—two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, and in-place cyclic/Dutch-flag partitioning—reduce naive $O(n^2)$ brute-force scans into linear $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space.
spark.keyTakeaway: Exploit ordering, monotonicity, or prefix invariants to trade nested loops for single-pass index movement.

concept.whyItMatters: Contiguous arrays underpin database column stores, network packet buffers, image processing, and technical interviews. Replacing an $O(n^2)$ nested loop with an $O(n)$ sliding window or prefix sum cuts 100,000-element processing from ~10 billion operations (~10s) down to ~100k operations (<1 ms) while avoiding heap allocations.
whenToUse: Two Pointers: finding pairs/triplets in sorted arrays, deduplicating in-place, or partitioning elements around a pivot in $O(1)$ space.
Sliding Window: computing longest/shortest contiguous subarrays satisfying a monotonic condition (e.g., sum $\le K$ with non-negative numbers, or $\le K$ distinct items).
Prefix Sums / Difference Arrays: answering $Q$ immutable range-sum queries in $O(1)$ each, or applying $Q$ range-increment updates in $O(1)$ each before a single $O(n)$ sweep.
whenNotToUse: Standard Sliding Window on arrays containing negative numbers for target-sum problems—shrinking the window is no longer monotonic; use Prefix Sum + HashMap instead.
Prefix Sums on arrays with frequent interleaved point updates and range queries—use a Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) or Segment Tree for $O(\log n)$ updates.
In-place array shifting (`insert`/`delete` at index `0`) in hot loops—prefer a ring buffer (`collections.deque`) or linked structure to avoid $O(n)$ memmove.
keyPoints: Opposite-direction Two Pointers (`left = 0`, `right = n - 1`) converge in $O(n)$ when the array is sorted or monotonic (e.g., Two Sum II, Container With Most Water).
Same-direction Two Pointers (`slow`, `fast`) compact or partition arrays in-place with $O(1)$ extra memory (e.g., Remove Duplicates, Move Zeroes, Dutch National Flag 3-way partition).

Sliding Window maintains a valid `[left, right]` invariant: expand `right` to explore, shrink `left` while the constraint is violated, achieving amortized $O(n)$ because each pointer moves at most $n$ times.
Prefix Sum `P[i] = P[i-1] + A[i-1]` turns `sum(l..r)` into `P[r+1] - P[l]`; pairing `P` with a HashMap (`count[P[r] - k]`) solves Subarray Sum Equals K with negative numbers in $O(n)$.
Difference Array `D[l] += v; D[r+1] -= v` batches $m$ range updates in $O(m)$ and reconstructs the final array with one $O(n)$ prefix sum pass.

examples.title: Subarray Sum Equals K with Negative Numbers (Python)
examples.scenario: Count contiguous subarrays summing to `k = 7` in `[3, 4, -7, 1, 3, 3, 1, -4]` where negative values break sliding-window monotonicity.
examples.outcome: Tracking running prefix sums in a HashMap `{0: 1}` checks `prefix - k` at each step, finding all 4 matching subarrays in $O(n)$ time and $O(n)$ space.

examples.title: In-Place 3-Way Partition / Dutch National Flag (Java)
examples.scenario: Sort an array of `0`s, `1`s, and `2`s in a single pass without `Arrays.sort()` ($O(n \log n)$) or counting-sort's two passes.
examples.outcome: Three pointers (`low`, `mid`, `high`) swap `0`s left and `2`s right while advancing `mid`, sorting in $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

tradeOffs.factor: In-Place Two Pointers vs. Auxiliary Array
tradeOffs.pro: $O(1)$ extra space and high CPU cache locality without heap allocation.
tradeOffs.con: Mutates the caller's input array and can be non-stable (relative order of equal elements may change).

tradeOffs.factor: Sliding Window vs. Prefix Sum + HashMap
tradeOffs.pro: Sliding window uses $O(1)$ or $O(K)$ space and avoids hash-table overhead.
tradeOffs.con: Breaks on negative numbers for sum constraints; Prefix Sum + HashMap handles arbitrary negatives in $O(n)$ space.

tradeOffs.pro: Difference array applies range updates in $O(1)$ with 5 lines of code.
tradeOffs.con: Only supports offline queries after all updates are applied; online interleaved queries need a Segment Tree or BIT.

failureModes.name: Off-by-One Boundary & Inclusive/Exclusive Confusion
failureModes.description: Mixing 0-indexed array bounds with `P[r+1] - P[l]` prefix indexing or `right - left + 1` window length causes `IndexOutOfBoundsException` or off-by-one counts.
failureModes.mitigation: Standardize on half-open intervals `[left, right)` or `P` of length `n + 1` with `P[0] = 0`.

failureModes.name: 32-Bit Integer Overflow in Prefix Sums
failureModes.description: Summing $10^5$ elements of $10^9$ overflows 32-bit `int` (max $\approx 2.14 \times 10^9$) in Java/C++, wrapping into negative numbers.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use 64-bit `long` for prefix sums, difference arrays, and running window sums.

failureModes.name: Applying Sliding Window to Non-Monotonic Data
failureModes.description: Shrinking `left` when `window_sum > k` skips valid subarrays if negative numbers appear later in the array.
failureModes.mitigation: Verify non-negativity before choosing a sliding window; otherwise switch to Prefix Sum + HashMap or a monotonic deque.

failureModes.name: Unbounded `while` Loop in Pointer Convergence
failureModes.description: Failing to advance `left++` or `right--` on equal branches in two-pointer loops triggers an infinite loop.
failureModes.mitigation: Ensure every branch inside `while (left < right)` strictly narrows `right - left`.

commonMistakes: Forgetting to initialize the prefix-sum HashMap with `{0: 1}`, missing subarrays that start at index `0`.
Sorting an array before running Two Pointers when the problem asks for original indices (must store `(value, index)` pairs first).
Using `del list[0]` or `ArrayList.remove(0)` inside a loop, turning an $O(n)$ algorithm into $O(n^2)$.
Modifying the difference array `D[r + 1] -= val` without allocating `n + 1` elements, causing out-of-bounds writes when `r == n - 1`.
Assuming `a + b` won't overflow `int` in binary-search midpoints or two-sum checks (`mid = left + (right - left) / 2`).

sections.content:
## The idea

Naive array algorithms often inspect every pair `(i, j)` or subarray `[i..j]`, costing $O(n^2)$ time. Array manipulation techniques eliminate redundant work by preserving **state across adjacent indices**. Whether moving two pointers inward on sorted data, sliding a monotonic window `[left, right]`, or precomputing cumulative prefix sums `P[i]`, each element is touched a constant number of times—bringing time complexity down to $O(n)$.

## Concrete walkthrough

Walk through **Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters** on `s = "abcabcbb"` using a Sliding Window + last-seen index map:

1. **Initialize**: `left = 0`, `best = 0`, `seen = {}`.
2. **Expand `right = 0..2`** (`'a', 'b', 'c'`): None are in `seen` at `>= left`. Window is `"abc"`, `best = 3`.
3. **Collision at `right = 3`** (`'a'`): `seen['a']` is `0` (`>= left`). Jump `left = seen['a'] + 1 = 1` (never move `left` backward!), update `seen['a'] = 3`. Window is `"bca"` (len 3).
4. **Continue to `right = 7`**: Each collision jumps `left` forward in $O(1)$ without scanning the characters in between. Total time: $O(n)$ for $n$ characters; space: $O(\min(n, |\Sigma|))$.

sections.content:
## In-place cyclic sort & Kadane's algorithm

Two specialized $O(n)$ / $O(1)$ patterns round out the toolkit:

- **Cyclic Sort**: When an array of length $n$ contains integers in `[1..n]` (or `[0..n-1]`), place each value `x` at index `x - 1` by swapping until `A[i] == A[A[i] - 1]`. Every swap puts at least one element in its final home, guaranteeing $\le n$ swaps total—ideal for finding missing or duplicate numbers in $O(1)$ space.
- **Kadane's Algorithm**: Computes the maximum subarray sum in one pass via `cur = max(x, cur + x); best = max(best, cur)`. Because a negative running prefix `cur < 0` can never improve any future subarray, resetting it to `x` is provably optimal.

## Pattern selection matrix

| Technique | Time | Extra Space | Key Precondition | Classic Problem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Opposite Two Pointers** | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ | Sorted or monotonic | Two Sum II, 3Sum, Rain Water |
| **Fast/Slow Pointers** | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ | In-place filter/partition | Remove Duplicates, Move Zeroes |
| **Sliding Window** | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$–$O(K)$ | Monotonic window validity | Longest Substring No Repeats |
| **Prefix Sum + HashMap** | $O(n)$ | $O(n)$ | Exact target sum (any sign) | Subarray Sum Equals K |
| **Difference Array** | $O(n + Q)$ | $O(n)$ | Offline range increments | Corporate Flight Bookings |
| **Cyclic Sort** | $O(n)$ | $O(1)$ | Values bounded in `[1..n]` | Find All Duplicates in Array |

## Failure modes

1. **Backward `left` Pointer in Sliding Window**: Setting `left = seen[ch] + 1` blindly without `max(left, seen[ch] + 1)` moves `left` backward into stale characters, inflating window length.
2. **Quadratic String/Slice Concatenation**: Building subarrays via `res += arr[l:r]` inside a loop turns an $O(n)$ pointer scan into $O(n^2)$ memory copies.
3. **Integer Overflow on `P[i]`**: Accumulating large positive integers into 32-bit `int` in Java silently wraps and breaks `P[r] - P[l]` comparisons.
4. **Mutating While Iterating**: Removing elements from a dynamic array mid-loop shifts indices and skips elements.

sections.eyebrow: 06 / From interview patterns to production systems
sections.content:
## From interview patterns to production systems

These exact primitives power real systems: **ring buffers** in LMAX Disruptor and Linux `io_uring` use two-pointer head/tail indices over fixed arrays for lock-free $O(1)$ IPC; **rate limiters** use sliding-window counters; and **columnar analytics engines** (DuckDB, ClickHouse) run vectorized prefix sums and SIMD scans over contiguous arrays to saturate memory bandwidth.

## Practical checklist

- **Check monotonicity first**: if adding elements can violate and removing elements can restore validity, use Sliding Window; if negatives break this, use Prefix Sum + HashMap.
- **Use `long` for sums**: always widen accumulators to 64-bit integers in statically typed languages.
- **Pad prefix arrays by 1**: allocate `P[n + 1]` with `P[0] = 0` so `sum(l, r) = P[r + 1] - P[l]` needs no `l == 0` special case.
- **Guard `left` monotonicity**: always write `left = max(left, ...)` when jumping pointers with a last-seen index map.
- **Test edge cases**: empty arrays (`[]`), single elements (`[x]`), all negatives, and duplicate values.

interviewProblems.title: Array Manipulation Techniques
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Array Manipulation Techniques. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Core array manipulation techniques—two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums, and in-place cyclic/Dutch-flag partitioning—reduce naive $O(n^2)$ brute-force scans into linear $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary space.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Prefix Sum / Diff Array applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Invariant / Answer.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Invariant / Answer experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Standardize on half-open intervals `[left, right)` or `P` of length `n + 1` with `P[0] = 0`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Exploit ordering, monotonicity, or prefix invariants to trade nested loops for single-pass index movement.
Avoid trap: Forgetting to initialize the prefix-sum HashMap with `{0: 1}`, missing subarrays that start at index `0`.
Avoid trap: Sorting an array before running Two Pointers when the problem asks for original indices (must store `(value, index)` pairs first).
When to reach for it: Two Pointers: finding pairs/triplets in sorted arrays, deduplicating in-place, or partitioning elements around a pivot in $O(1)$ space.
When to reach for it: Sliding Window: computing longest/shortest contiguous subarrays satisfying a monotonic condition (e.g., sum $\le K$ with non-negative numbers, or $\le K$ distinct items).
